findings.fix: Confirm the polarity is intended, or add a pull resistor that holds the gate at its safe (OFF) level until the firmware drives it.
findings.what: Control net 'GATE_CTRL' may be energised at power-up
findings.why: 'GATE_CTRL' drives a transistor/relay, is driven HIGH and held from power-up, and has no resistor setting a safe default. If a HIGH turns the switched load ON when it must stay OFF until firmware enables it, it is energised at power-up.

findings.fix: Fix the copper short(s) named in the DRC section, then re-analyze to see the healthy-board behaviour.
findings.what: This co-sim ran WITH the board's 1 copper short bridged into the circuit.
findings.why: The DRC section above found copper from separate nets touching. The co-sim applies those bridges before simulating, so the rail and GPIO voltages below reflect the board as it would actually be built, not an idealised un-shorted version of it.

findings.fix: Find and remove the bridge (see the copper-spacing / DRC report for the exact spot), or, if the connection is intended, make them one named net deliberately.
findings.what: SHORT:+5V-GND is involved in a short (two nets bridged together).
findings.why: Two connections that should be separate are tied together, so they are forced to the same voltage. If one is a power rail this can dump large current through the short and overheat parts.

report.headline: 3 issues found, 2 serious. Fix the serious ones before ordering boards.

findings.fix: Pull the two pieces of copper apart so there is a clear gap between them, or remove the bit of copper that bridges them. If they really are supposed to connect, give them the same net name.
findings.what: Two separate connections, "GND" and "+5V", are touching, near x=112.0 mm, y=100.0 mm on the back copper layer (B.Cu).
findings.why: These are meant to be electrically separate. Where they touch they become one connection (a short), so "GND" and "+5V" will be forced to the same voltage. That usually means the board does the wrong thing, and if one is a power rail it can pull large current and overheat.
